⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s Christmas morning.
  • Sources indicate that maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate.
  • In a recent development, in fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It has been revealed that it’s Christmas morning. The street outside is still, your phone hasn’t buzzed with plans, and the whole day is wide open, with no schedule and no one to check in with. It might feel like a relief, or it might ache. Sometimes it’s both in the same hour.

Sources indicate that maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate. But no matter why you’re spending Christmas alone, the day can still feel warm and full.

In a recent development, in fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own. Here you’ll find ideas for staying in or going out, plus what to do if it gets hard.

If you’re spending Christmas on your own, you’re far from the only one. More people live alone than ever, and plenty of people simply prefer a quiet holiday.

Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, being alone and feeling lonely aren't the same thing. Being alone is a circumstance: no one else is around. Loneliness is a feeling of disconnection, and it can show up at a packed holiday table or an empty house.

In a recent development, so what makes time alone feel good rather than lonely? A massive factor may be whether you have a say in how you spend it. In three studies where people reported on their moments throughout the day, time alone felt more positive when people chose it for themselves.

If you didn’t choose to be alone this Christmas, it’s okay if that stings. What you do with the day is still up to you.

Whether you’re in the mood for a slow day under a blanket, time out among people, or a bit of both, you don’t owe anyone an explanation for how you spend your day.

If you’d rather stay in, here are a few ways to make the day at home feel comforting.

It has been revealed that 1. Start the morning with meditation or journaling: Settle into a comfortable position and let your eyes close or soften. Tune into your breath and the sensations in your body. When thoughts about the day ahead drift in, notice them, then gently return to your breath. Journaling is another way to check in with how you’re feeling.

In a recent development, 💙 Want some guidance for those few minutes? Settle into the Mornings meditation on Calm.

2. Cook or order the meal you really want: Skip the turkey-and-trimmings unless you love them. Go for whatever you're craving, whether that’s a roast for one, pancakes at noon, or your go-to takeout. Choosing food you’re excited about can turn an ordinary meal into a treat.

💙 Listen to Piano for Rainy Days: Nice & Cozy while you cook.

It has been revealed that 4. Do a movie marathon on your own terms: You get to choose what you watch, and no one talks through the good parts. Line up your favorite holiday films, or skip the Christmas theme entirely and binge the series you’ve been saving.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Get lost in a book or an audiobook: A long, quiet day is a great chance to sink into a story without interruption. If your eyes get tired, switch to an audiobook while you putter around or lie on the couch.

💙 Discover ten self-love activities to improve your well-being.

If you’d like to spend the day out of the house, these ideas include solo outings and activities around other people. Holiday hours often change and volunteer spots fill up, so check details as early as you can..

6. Spend time somewhere green: Stroll along a park path or trail, or find a bench and settle in for a while. Time in green space has been shown to quiet a busy mind. In one study, adults who walked for 90 minutes in nature reported less rumination (the looping, negative thinking that can feed low moods) than those who walked along a busy road.

Industry observers note that 💙 Ready to step outside? Try Calm’s Nature Walk meditation with Dr. Eric López to soak in the sights, sounds, and smells around you.

7. Volunteer for a few hours: Soup kitchens, shelters, and animal rescues often need extra hands on Christmas Day. Volunteering connects you with people who share a purpose, and research suggests performing acts of kindness may boost your well-being.

💙 Feeling the urge to give back? Tune into the Random Acts of Kindness meditation on Calm to see how small gestures add up.

Recent findings suggest that 8. Join a community meal or gathering: Many community centers and local groups host open Christmas meals. It’s a low-pressure way to share the day with others, even if only for a couple of hours.

Recent findings suggest that 9. Find somewhere that’s open: Movie theaters, some cafés and restaurants, and hotel lounges often keep holiday hours. Even a little time around other people, strangers included, can bring a touch of connection to your day.

10. Take a day trip: Head to a nearby town, hike a upcoming trail, or visit a spot you’ve been meaning to see. A change of scenery can make the day feel like an occasion.

There are many ways to make a quiet day feel less lonely, from a quick text to a mindfulness practice. Choose whichever of these appeal to you.

Industry observers note that send a text, leave a voice note, or call someone you care about. If loved ones are far away, you could:.

Schedule a call in advance, especially if you’re in different time zones.

Do an activity together over video, like cooking or watching a movie.

Ask for a family recipe, make it, and share how it turned out.

Sources indicate that you can start a tradition on your own. Keep it small and simple, such as a letter to your future self you open next year or a movie you rewatch every December 25.

💙 Not sure where to start? Explore Redefining Traditions with therapist Kati Morton on Calm.

According to recent reports, if you feel loneliness creeping in, a loving-kindness meditation may help you feel more connected. In one study, people who did a short loving-kindness meditation reported more feelings of social connection toward strangers than those who did a control task.

💙 Press play on the Loving-Kindness meditation on Calm.

In a recent development, give yourself one thing to look forward to after your shift, such as a comfort meal or a call with someone you love. Treat yourself during the day with a good coffee or a walk on your break. You can also celebrate with others on another day, and it’s just as meaningful.

💙 If you’re still feeling lonely after the holiday, here are seven tips to deal with loneliness.

Recent findings suggest that even if you’ve chosen to be alone, Christmas can bring up emotions like sadness, envy, or grief. Here’s how to work through them.

Other people’s picture-perfect holiday photos can leave you feeling like you’re missing out. Try stepping away from your phone for a few hours. Those posts are a highlight reel, and the rest of their day rarely looks as polished.

If the feeling lingers, try self-compassion: meeting yourself with the same warmth you’d offer a friend who’s feeling down. In a review of studies, people who practiced self-compassion reported lower anxiety, depression, and stress than people who didn’t. You could tell yourself, “This is hard, but I’m doing my best, and that’s enough.”.

💙 Practice being a Friend on the Inside with Jeff Warren on Calm.

In a recent development, if you’re missing someone this Christmas, the day can feel especially tender. You can honor them in subtle ways: cook their favorite dish, light a candle in their memory, or write them a letter. There’s no right way to grieve, so let the day be as quiet or as full as you need.

It’s okay to keep some distance from family on Christmas if you need to. Calls and replies are optional, and so is explaining your choice. You can mute the group chat for the day if that brings you some peace.

If someone asks what you’re up to, you could say, “I’m keeping it low-key this year.” Whatever comes up, mixed feelings included, you don’t have to push it aside just because it’s the holidays.

According to recent reports, if your sadness lingers past the holiday, disrupts your sleep or appetite, or leaves you feeling hopeless, talk to a doctor or someone you trust. If you’re in the U.S. and need support right away, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. If you’re outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists free local services.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re alone for Christmas, it can help to give the day some structure. Pick one or two things that excite you, such as a comfort meal, a long walk, or a movie, and let the rest of the day unfold naturally. A quick call or text with a loved one can be a nice touch, too.

According to recent reports, it’s normal to want to spend Christmas alone. After a long or busy year, a quiet day can be restful, and preferring it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. Plan the day around what appeals to you.

If you’d rather not stay home on Christmas, there are plenty of places to spend the day. Look for open movie theaters, cafés, and parks nearby, or join a community meal at a local center. You could also volunteer for an organization to meet people while contributing to a cause. Holiday hours vary, so it’s worth confirming before you head out.

According to recent reports, if you’re single on Christmas, the day is yours to spend however you want. You could cook something you love, explore a upcoming spot, or go for a casual meal or movie with friends.

Industry observers note that if you’re feeling sad or lonely on Christmas, let yourself feel those emotions without judgment. Consider reaching out to a loved one, even briefly. A short meditation can also bring some relief. If the sadness feels overwhelming or won’t lift, speak to a doctor or someone you trust.

It’s okay to skip Christmas altogether. You can treat December 25 as an ordinary day: rest, work, or do something unrelated to the holiday. If the season stirs up grief or stress, stepping back from holiday looks is one way to look after yourself.

A solo tradition can be anything that brings you comfort, whether that’s a special breakfast, a journal entry, or a new ornament you pick out every year. A simple tradition is more likely to stick from year to year.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

Breaking: ADHD in Midlife & Beyond: 5 Big Research Findings

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.
  • The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.
  • An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.

The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.

An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records. Missed diagnoses and misdiagnoses make research on this population difficult — but not impossible.

Amber John, Ph.D., a researcher at the University of Liverpool, reviewed studies on how the experience of ADHD changes with age during her November 2026 ADDitude webinar, “Aging with ADHD: Newly introduced Research Findings in Midlife and Beyond.”.

Below are some of the themes John highlighted and what they suggest about the support adults with ADHD need in midlife and beyond.

In clinical interviews, adults with ADHD recalled feeling different growing up but being unable to explain why. A diagnosis helped them see those experiences in a different light.

It has been revealed that “These experiences that previously might have seemed disconnected, for many, started to form this more understandable pattern,” John said. “And that could really change the meaning that someone gives to those past experiences, particularly where they had just been viewed as evidence of personal failings.”.

[Read: The Transformative Power of an ADHD Diagnosis for Older Women].

According to recent reports, many people with ADHD develop painstaking routines and coping strategies to manage symptoms. The effort it takes to keep those routines going often goes unseen and can fuel burnout.

Industry observers note that “This raises a really key question about what it is that we actually mean when we say someone is functioning well,” John said. “Understanding someone’s support needs really means that we need to ask about the cost of managing.”.

Industry observers note that the experience of ADHD changes as life circumstances change. Menopause, caring for aging parents, and retirement can affect how symptoms play out in daily life and disrupt routines that have helped people cope for decades.

“A way that somebody is using to manage or to cope that’s worked in one period of life might become less useful when health, or demands, or available support changes,” John stated.

Sources indicate that [Read: I Feared I Had Alzheimer’s. It Turns Out It Was Undiagnosed ADHD.].

Sources indicate that in doctors’ offices and workplaces, people with ADHD often shoulder the burden of explaining their needs and advocating for basic support. They can put considerable effort into managing their symptoms and still face barriers to getting care or participating at work.

“There is a limit to focusing on individual-level coping because a person can put really substantial effort into managing whilst the environment actually continues to make participation difficult,” John noted.

According to recent reports, john’s research highlights the need for ADHD support that adapts as people’s circumstances change. We shouldn’t assume that “what helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s,” she remarked.

#137895. Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2567 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Sources indicate that you’re finally on the other side of the panic attack.
  • The hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Sources indicate that you’re finally on the other side of the panic attack. The chest tightness has eased, the shaking has stopped, and your breathing feels more steady. But instead of relief, there’s a strange exhaustion settling in, like you just ran a marathon you don’t remember signing up for. This is often called a panic attack hangover.

The hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting. You might experience headaches, sore muscles, difficulty concentrating, or an overwhelming need to crash. These symptoms can feel alarming if no one ever mentioned they might show up, but they’re actually a normal part of the body’s recovery process.

Recent findings suggest that understanding what’s happening can ease some of the worry, and having a few gentle tools on hand can make the aftermath feel a little less isolating. Here’s what to know about panic attack hangovers, along with research-backed tips to support yourself through them.

Recent findings suggest that A panic attack hangover is the period of lingering after-effects that follow a panic attack. Even though the rush of fear and physical symptoms has eased, your body can still feel off-balance for hours or even days afterward. Many people describe it as feeling strangely similar to an alcohol hangover: foggy, heavy, and emotionally sensitive.

According to recent reports, the experience can be unsettling, especially if you didn’t expect panic to have an “aftermath.” But panic attack hangovers are both common and temporary. They’re simply your body’s way of recovering from an intense stress response.

Note: This guide focuses on panic attacks. If you’ve had an anxiety attack, which builds more gradually, read How to manage symptoms and find ease after an anxiety attack instead.

Sources indicate that while panic attack hangovers can happen at any time, the effects aren’t the same for everyone. Still, there are some common symptoms people notice after a panic attack, some more frequently than others.

Fatigue or exhaustion: You might feel like your body’s battery has been completely drained.

Brain fog: You could find it hard to focus, remember things, or think clearly.

Muscle tension or soreness: Your jaw, shoulders, or chest might feel tight, achy, or tender from holding too much stress.

Emotional sensitivity: You may notice yourself crying more easily or feeling unusually fragile in everyday situations.

Headaches: You might experience pressure or pain often triggered by stress, shallow breathing, or unconscious clenching.

Digestive issues: You could have nausea, stomach discomfort, or sudden changes in your appetite that don’t seem to track.

Sleepiness or difficulty sleeping: You may find yourself crashing hard into deep rest or lying awake because you’re unable to settle down.

Industry observers note that these symptoms usually fade within a day, although they can last longer depending on the amount of sleep you get, your stress levels, and your overall health. If they’re frequent or overwhelming, though, it may be a sign to get additional support.

The reason panic leaves a hangover comes down to how your body handles stress. A panic attack sends your nervous system into full alert: your heart races, your breath quickens, and your muscles tighten. This is an ancient survival mechanism that’s been designed to keep you safe in an emergency.

In a recent development, the problem? Even when the threat isn’t real, your body still goes through the motions without an outlet to use up that surge of energy.

Once the attack ends, your system shifts into recovery mode. That crash can leave you feeling shaky, sore, and depleted… much like finishing an intense workout. On top of that, the emotional weight of the experience—fear, vulnerability, or the worry it might happen again—can keep your brain buzzing even while your body’s trying to rest.

This combination of physical exhaustion and emotional strain creates the foggy, heavy state that many people call a panic attack hangover.

According to recent reports, related read: Panic attack vs. anxiety attack? Here's the difference.

Industry observers note that panic attack hangovers can hit you hard, and you may not have the energy to do much after. These ideas are simple, low-lift, and designed for the days when everything feels like just too much.

Pick what’s doable today and ignore the rest: your nervous system will get the memo.

Your body just ran an internal marathon, and it’s important to be kind to it. If you can, postpone non-urgent tasks and try to give yourself a small recovery window.

Recent findings suggest that set a 10–15 minute timer, lie down or sit with support behind your back, and let your eyes rest. If you’re at work, try a short break, plus two minutes of slow breathing in a quiet corner. A pause can often help you recover faster.

Recent findings suggest that related read: Stressed and short on time? Here's how to try micro-meditation.

Industry observers note that staying hydrated and keeping your blood sugar steady can help you feel more balanced as your body recovers from a panic attack. Dehydration and dips in blood sugar can make fatigue, headaches, and brain fog worse.

Drink water or an electrolyte beverage and have a simple snack, like fruit with nut butter, yogurt, or toast. This helps give your system some fuel to reset.

Slow, gentle breathing tells your nervous system that you’re safe. Try this for 2–3 minutes: Inhale through your nose for four counts, and then exhale through pursed lips for six or eight.

Industry observers note that longer exhales can help your nervous system shift from fight-or-flight into rest-and-digest mode. But only do this if you feel comfortable. Don’t try to force anything.

💙 If you need some guidance, check out Reset with the Breath with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Panic can cause you to tighten your muscles, especially in the jaw, chest, shoulders, and hands. Short, light movements help clear it all without overexertion.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to do anything too intense. Simple shoulder rolls, gentle neck circles, a slow doorframe chest stretch, or a five-minute walk around the block or office floor can all help. If you’re seated, simply unclench your jaw, open and close your hands 10 times, or shake out your arms. The point is to loosen everything up.

According to recent reports, 💙 Need a little extra support? Try the Softening Anxiety Daily Move session with Mel Mah on the Calm app.

Quick temperature shifts, like splashing cool water on your face or holding something cold, can help ground you and interrupt the leftover jitters after a panic attack.

This is because it’s actually a form of grounding that allows your nervous system to anchor itself back to the present moment.

Related read: 18 grounding techniques to help relieve anxiety.

Decision fatigue amplifies the brain fog that comes after a panic attack, so try to cut down on the number of choices you’re making.

Trim your to-do list to one or two essentials, and choose “good enough” over perfect. Reheat leftovers instead of cooking, tell your coworkers you’re running a little behind, and move all noncritical tasks to the next day. It sounds simple, but having that space will help more than you know.

According to recent reports, reduce stimulation to ease the post-panic attack stress. Dim overhead lights, switch to warm lamps, lower the volume on any music or background noise, and silence non-urgent notifications on your phone and laptop for an hour.

Recent findings suggest that if noise is unavoidable, try earplugs or a brown-noise playlist. If you enjoy aromatherapy a familiar scent (like lavender, vanilla, or eucalyptus) can also be grounding.

Writing a few lines about your feelings and symptoms post-panic attack can help your brain process what happened and move forward. Research indicates that journaling supports emotional regulation, which is why so many people find it useful for panic recovery, too — even if it’s just a quick note or voice memo.

Recent findings suggest that consider reflecting on what triggered your attack, what symptoms you noticed, what helped calm you down, and what you could do differently next time. This can help give you more effective coping tools for future attacks.

Reaching out, even with a simple text, helps calm the nervous system. Social support is one of the strongest buffers for stress recovery.

In a recent development, send a text to someone you trust, simply asking to check in. If talking feels like too much, having someone just sit with you can also be helpful.

Related read: How to help someone having a panic attack (and what to avoid).

It has been revealed that after a panic attack, your system is more sensitive. Consider skipping or reducing how much caffeine you drink, as it can re-spark jitters. And avoid alcohol, as it’s been known to disrupt sleep and mood. Swap in decaf, herbal tea, or a half-caf and make sure to focus on nutrition and hydration to help support recovery.

Recent findings suggest that fatigue after a panic attack is real, and quality sleep helps reset your stress response. Keep bedtime predictable with a wind-down routine you enjoy, darken the room, and cool it slightly.

Recent findings suggest that if you desperately need a nap, cap it at 20–30 minutes, and avoid late-evening naps in order to protect nighttime sleep. If your mind spins when it’s time to go to bed, try a quiet meditation or body scan. This can help quiet the mind long enough to help you drift off faster.

💙 Fall asleep with ease thanks to the White Noise soundscape on the Calm app.

According to recent reports, even just knowing what you’ll do next time can take the edge off that heavy, shaky feeling that lingers after a panic attack. One simple idea? Make a three-step proposal that you keep on your phone or in your wallet.

Spend two minutes on long exhales or humming.

Splash cold water on your face or run cool water over your wrists.

It also helps to add one contact you trust to call or text.

While you may not be able to prevent every spiral, it always helps to have something in your back pocket (literally) that helps you feel less alone and more ready.

Yes, a hangover can sometimes trigger panic attacks. This is because alcohol disrupts sleep, dehydrates your body, and causes blood sugar swings — and all of these effects can make your nervous system more sensitive the next day.

Sources indicate that alcohol also interferes with the neurotransmitters that regulate your mood, which can amplify feelings of unease or dread. If you’re already prone to anxiety, that extra stress can tip into panic.

Every person who drinks won’t necessarily have a panic attack, but if you notice a pattern between hangovers and panic, it may help to cut back, hydrate more intentionally, or avoid drinking on nights before demanding days.

For most people, the hungover feeling eases within a few hours, but it’s not unusual for fatigue or brain fog to stretch into the next day. The duration of a panic attack hangover depends on several factors: how intense the panic attack was, how long it lasted, how well you slept, and what kind of support you gave your body afterward.

Try to find the recovery initiative that works best for you: getting enough water, food, gentle movement, and rest can speed up the reset. However, if you find that your hangover lasts longer than 24 hours or happens every time you panic, it may be a sign that your nervous system is under strain. In this case, getting some professional support can help.

Brain fog and fatigue are your nervous system’s way of asking for recovery time, so supporting your body can make the fog lift faster. Start with water or an electrolyte drink, followed by a small, balanced meal or snack. Light movement like walking or stretching also helps by boosting circulation and clearing leftover stress hormones, while short breaks from screens give your brain a reset.

Some people find that changing environments—stepping outside for fresh air, moving to a quieter space, or dimming harsh lighting—makes a noticeable difference in clarity. Rest is important, too, but you don’t want to overdo it. A short nap capped at 20–30 minutes usually helps more than staying in bed for hours.

The exhaustion you feel after a panic attack is the crash that comes after an adrenaline surge. Basically, when you panic, your body burns through enormous amounts of energy in a short time. Your heart rate rises, your muscles tense, and your brain goes into overdrive to scan for danger.

Even though there isn’t an actual threat, your body doesn’t know that, so it uses up its resources as if there is. Once the panic attack passes, your hormones shift, and your body needs to come down from the emotional intensity. While it’s easy to look at this exhaustion as weakness, it’s really just your body’s way of recovering from an all-systems-on alert. That’s why gentleness is key for recovery.

In a recent development, you can’t always prevent panic attacks, but you can definitely soften the after-effects. The most helpful strategies are proactive, or preventing one before it comes on. Think: getting consistent sleep, eating balanced meals to keep blood sugar steady, staying hydrated, and limiting alcohol or excessive caffeine.

Recent findings suggest that some people find it useful to have a short aftercare routine ready, too, such as hydrating, stretching, or texting a friend once the panic subsides. This helps to prevent the hangover from stretching out longer than necessary.

It has been revealed that over time, therapy and skills training can also reduce both the frequency of panic attacks and the severity of hangovers. You’ll essentially learn how to give your nervous system a softer landing.

Industry observers note that headaches and sore muscles are common after a panic attack. During panic, your jaw, neck, shoulders, and chest may tighten without you noticing, and fast, shallow breathing could add to the headache.

Unclenching your jaw, rolling your shoulders, or holding a cool compress to your forehead may help. Get care right away if you have a sudden, severe headache, chest pain, numbness or weakness, trouble speaking, or vision changes. If your headache lasts longer than you’d expect, check in with your doctor or primary care provider.

Recent findings suggest that after a panic attack, give your body a few minutes to settle before you do anything else. Stay where you are if it’s safe, and take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale.

In a recent development, shakiness or fog is a normal part of coming down from panic, so you don’t need to push through it. Once the first wave passes, tell someone you trust what happened and lower the demands on yourself for the rest of the day. The 12 tips above have ideas for the hours that follow. If panic attacks keep happening, talking with a doctor or mental health professional may help.

Tech Report: Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a latest study.
  • Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.
  • The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a latest study.

Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1.

The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.

According to recent reports, study participants self-reported the severity of premenstrual symptoms, such as irritability and fatigue, and the intensity of period pain (categorized as mild, moderate, or severe). Findings indicated that severe menstrual pain was associated with higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptoms.

In a recent development, premenstrual symptoms demonstrated a graded pattern in their association with mental health outcomes. Mild premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety symptom scores. Moderate premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety and depression symptom scores. Severe premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores.

The researchers offered several social and biological factors as potential explanations for these results.

“Psychosocially, menstrual pain and [premenstrual symptoms] may result in functional impairment – including missed school, disrupted sleep, reduced social participation – which may contribute to emotional distress,” they wrote.

Sources indicate that the study explained that intense period pain and premenstrual distress may activate inflammatory and pain-sensitivity pathways, increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression. Researchers also noted that the neurobiological mechanisms for processing pain may overlap with those involved in attention and focus, which could help explain the connection between menstrual pain and ADHD symptoms.

In a recent development, researchers also suggested that fluctuating estrogen and progesterone may help to explain the connection between severe premenstrual symptoms and higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores. These hormones heavily affect serotonin, dopamine, and GABA in the brain. Serotonin is linked to mood; dopamine controls motivation and reward processing; and GABA is crucial for emotional processing and regulation. When hormones fluctuate before a menstrual cycle, these neurotransmitters are impacted too, which, in turn, may influence symptoms of anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

It has been revealed that the relationship between ADHD and hormonal fluctuations is a pressing subject for many ADDitude readers with lived experience. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 2,000 women with ADHD, almost one in two respondents noted that hormonal fluctuations had a “life-altering” or “severe” impact on their ADHD.

“I know that the week before my period I am a complete mess,” Addison, an ADDitude reader, said. “I have to prepare for the fact that my world feels like it’s falling apart emotionally, and I hate the way that I look the most that week. These are weeks I often avoid being with people, as I know I am not the most positive and am the most sensitive.”.

“I used to have lots of irritability, food cravings, tiredness, and was fuzzy-headed three to four days before my period started,” said Connie, another reader.

“I suffer from symptoms like uncontrolled fits of anger and crying spells and feeling extremely overwhelmed the days before my period. I’m even more moody, irritable and have more trouble concentrating,” said ADDitude reader Elena.

Moreover, women with ADHD are disproportionately affected by premenstrual disorders with more than 40% of women with ADHD experiencing premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) compared to 3% to 9% of women overall.2, 3 PMDD is also heavily tied to hormonal shifts and mental health.

“PMDD is caused by a high sensitivity to fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone, as well as decreases in serotonin – hormonal changes that happen during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle,” wrote Dara Abraham, D.O. in an ADDitude article. “During the luteal phase that follows ovulation, estrogen decreases, as do dopamine, serotonin, and eventually progesterone. These changes cause painful and distressing symptoms until the menstruation begins and hormone levels rise again.”.

The study also found that irregular menstrual cycles were linked to higher depression and anxiety symptom scores. The longer a girl had been having her menstrual cycles, the stronger the link between irregular periods and depression and anxiety symptoms became. Likewise, earlier age at menarche was associated with higher depression symptom scores.

While the study focused specifically on early age at menarche, previous research suggests that early puberty more broadly may have an association to ADHD.

Sources indicate that “Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children,” wrote Molly Nikolas, Ph.D. in an ADDitude article. “In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.”.

According to recent reports, the researchers listed several limitations to the study. Menstrual cycle characteristics were gathered through an annual self-report, and parents reported mental health symptoms. In addition, the relationship between menstrual characteristics and mental health symptoms may be bidirectional. The researchers also reported the associations were modest and that future studies are needed to further explore the potential social and biological mechanisms involved.

The study’s authors said they hope their findings will help healthcare professionals consider menstrual cycle characteristics as potentially meaningful insight when evaluating the mental health of adolescent girls.

How to Make Better Decisions in the Age of AI

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds.
  • It has been revealed that AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it.
  • Industry observers note that she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more crucial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds. The power of that little “Ask anything” AI prompt box is immense, but can it help us make wiser decisions? Cheryl Strauss Einhorn, author of The Human Edge: Smarter Decisions in the Age of AI, writes:.

It has been revealed that AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it. It can illuminate pathways we might not have seen or narrow our choices in ways we do not fully recognize. As AI systems become more integrated into our lives, the challenge is no longer simply about harnessing their power but about leading them with clarity, discernment, and commitment to human agency.

Industry observers note that she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more crucial. We spoke with her about why human judgment is a competitive advantage, how to engage our values when we prompt AI, and how AI can help us clarify our thinking.

Kia Afcari: You argue that AI makes human judgment more, not less, important. How can we make sure that the values of kindness and care are reflected when we use AI to help us make decisions?

Cheryl Strauss Einhorn: AI has no values. It has biases and influences by those who have designed it, and from whatever information has been fed into it. So to be sure that prosocial values are reflected when we use AI, we humans need to bring them into the work that we do together.

When working with an AI tool, we want to be asking ourselves, What is the problem that I’m solving? Why am I solving it? What is the context? And so we really need to be intentional with AI, because without asking ourselves those things first, AI doesn’t know why we’re coming to it.

Before you actually sit down with a tool, you can muster those values and those key factors related to the problem that you’re solving, and then articulate them and communicate them to the machine.

If we let the machine think for us, we can lose that sense of right and wrong, for example, because we actually care about all of those details that AI can’t possibly know about the problems that we’re solving and the people that we’re solving those problems with and for.

For example, you might ask yourself or your AI tool: Before I act, help me think through the people, relationships, and responsibilities this decision affects—not just the outcome it produces.

This type of human-centric AI interaction helped Felice, a food scientist at a pet food company, who was responsible for developing latest recipes that balance nutrition, taste, and market trends. She often has to delegate tasks within her research team, ensuring that product testing, ingredient sourcing, and regulatory compliance all move forward smoothly. Using AI, she was able to analyze workloads and expertise that suggested the best person for each task, but only Felice understood the deeper dynamics at play—who works best under tight deadlines, who has a passion for innovative formulations, and who needs mentorship. When AI recommended assigning a crucial stability test to her most experienced technician, this prompt supported her thinking about a different option: giving it to the junior scientist who was eager to develop his skills in quality assurance. The AI tool’s choices made sense based on efficiency, but Felice’s decision ensured both short-term success and long-term team development.

Recent findings suggest that KA: In the book, your “cheetah” metaphor celebrates slowing down. Why is a strategic pause so key when working with AI?

Recent findings suggest that CSE: The cheetah metaphor relates that although this is an animal that goes zero to 60 in about three seconds, its hunting prowess actually comes from being able to decelerate up to nine miles an hour in a single stride. And the reason why that’s so vital in problem solving and decision making is that’s where you build agility, flexibility, and maneuverability. Do I want to stay the course, or do I want to pivot and do something else?

This pause allows you to chunk your learning and pry open that cognitive space for latest information and insight. With an AI tool, it’s so crucial because there’s a difference between speed and quality.

When something truly matters to us, we want to make sure that we’re solving the problem in a way that solves it holistically, that takes care of the people who are involved in the problem with us. And when we’re moving really rapidly, sometimes those very crucial factors are hard to bring forward. So there’s a real difference between what is efficient and what is effective.

KA: Why can having more information make it harder—not easier—to make good decisions?

CSE: Francis Bacon once noted, “Knowledge is power,” but that’s not really true anymore, right? We now have all of the answers with AI to a lot of commonly asked questions and some uncommon questions.

We need to make sure we’re defining the problem that we’re solving, that we are understanding and communicating the motivation and providing the context, because you don’t want all the information. Otherwise, we’re going to end up with analysis paralysis.

Industry observers note that one thing people can use is what I call the “vision of success” question. This question asks you to time travel, to jump over the decision to see that the decision has been made well. What’s happening? What are those few things that if they don’t succeed, the decision fails? It’s actually very powerful, because it allows you to clearly identify so that you can articulate those factors that you absolutely need to be able to share with AI. These become the constraints and boundaries that set the perimeter around the decision, so that it can give you research that’s targeted and focused on those things.

According to recent reports, for example, Max deciding where to spend his next vacation. Asking AI for help directly—without turning to himself first—he got a list of destinations, airline options, and local attractions, complete with ratings, reviews, and price comparisons. On paper, that sounds ideal. But in reality, Max swiftly found himself paralyzed by the sheer amount of information. What if he picked a less-than-perfect hotel? What if he overlooked a hidden gem? AI has handed him a mountain of data, but it didn’t necessarily make the decision any easier.

However, when he used the “vision of success” question, he was able to realize and to share with his AI tool: “I want to return home feeling genuinely rested, having spent quality time with my family, without overspending or feeling like I missed the experience I was hoping for.”.

Only then does AI have a meaningful problem to solve. Instead of searching for the “best” vacation—a question with no objective answer—it can help Max find the destination most likely to produce the outcome he actually wants. AI can’t define success but it can optimize for the success you define.

KA: How does the AREA method help people make wiser decisions, especially when AI is involved? CSE: AREA is more than an acronym—it’s a framework for challenging our assumptions and thinking mistakes, and actively includes the perspectives of others. It stands for Absolute, Relative, Exploration and Exploitation, and Analysis.

According to recent reports, the first “A,” Absolute, focuses on primary, unfiltered information straight from primary sources. “R,” Relative, shifts to external viewpoints—secondary sources connected to the subject. “E,” Exploration and Exploitation, fuels creativity: Exploration broadens research through interviews and unconventional sources, while Exploitation turns inward, challenging personal biases and assumptions. The final “A,” Analysis, synthesizes everything, bringing clarity and structure to complex decisions.

When using AI, a system like AREA becomes even more key because AI doesn’t eliminate bias—it can reflect and sometimes amplify biases in its training data, design, and the way we use it. Good decisions require a process that helps us recognize and challenge both AI’s biases and our own.

According to recent reports, for AI, so much of the information, for example, is from Reddit. Information can be incomplete or outdated, and you also know that you’re interacting with a liar. It’s a machine that just gives you answers that are wrong sometimes.

So you need to be able to have a quality due diligence process to not only be able to use the tool effectively, but to be able to evaluate its outcome. Too often, people look at an answer with AI and think that it’s a transaction, and they can just take it. AREA is going to help you make sure that it’s a conversation. So you have an evidence-based perspective that has looked at a variety of stakeholder viewpoints, and made sure that you have pried open that cognitive space to challenge the natural, well-worn mental pathways that we all lean on every day.

KA: How can we use AI in ways that strengthen—rather than undermine—our values and agency?

Industry observers note that CSE: It’s a great question. I think the upcoming competitive advantage is going to be self-awareness.

This is the first tool that actually asks for some of our cognitive load; it wants us to offload some of our decisions to it. And this is a machine fundamentally about decision making, because we ask it for something and it gives us an answer. But there’s a very interesting invitation here, which is to each of us to get to know ourselves better.

According to recent reports, we each have a special sauce, which is the way that we make our decisions, and we make thousands of them every single day. But most of us have not sat down and said to themselves, What does that process actually look like? Can I actually name those pieces and put language to it?

Recent findings suggest that there is this invitation to get to know our thinking so that we can translate it better, and not only for the tool. How helpful would it be in conversation with our colleagues to be able to say clearly, This is how I’m actually going through the steps, this is how I’m thinking about it, these are the variables that I’m prioritizing, and here’s what I think is the most diagnostic.

You can think about your thinking skills as muscles. If we turn over our cognitive load, we will also weaken it. But if we actually take this invitation to understand our self-awareness and our metacognition, we can make sure that we strengthen those tools.

AI is a tool that has so many implications for our environment and for our world, in addition to the fact that it has implications for our actual thinking skills.

So I would say that the invitation is to turn to yourself first. Ask yourself why you’re using the tool, and whether or not you should be turning to yourself instead. And either way, bring your own thinking forward before sitting down, so that you can feel far more comfortable that you can problem-solve both with it and beyond it.

How to write your retirement message or announcement at work

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, retirement is the end of an era.
  • Sources indicate that to bring a sense of closure, many people like to write a message of gratitude to their colleagues before they sign off for the last time.
  • Nobody wants the stress of staring at a blinking cursor, so here are a few tips for announcing your retirement and writing a thoughtful goodbye message to the people you’ve worked with.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, retirement is the end of an era. And while it’s thrilling to finally have time to do all the things you’ve been meaning to do, leaving behind your coworkers, especially if you’re close, can feel bittersweet.

Sources indicate that to bring a sense of closure, many people like to write a message of gratitude to their colleagues before they sign off for the last time. But what do you say? How can you possibly sum up years of collaboration, chaos, and connection in just a few sentences?

Nobody wants the stress of staring at a blinking cursor, so here are a few tips for announcing your retirement and writing a thoughtful goodbye message to the people you’ve worked with. By adapting them to fit your specific role and personality, you can acknowledge the relationships that mattered, offer an authentic goodbye, and leave with intention. Happy retirement!

You might think that your retirement messages need to be a perfect balance of professional, funny, and sweet, but what’s most crucial is that you sound like yourself.

To ensure that your note is polished and professional, keep these tips in mind.

Recent findings suggest that most people don’t want to read a long email, no matter who it’s from. A few honest lines work perfectly.

Sources indicate that “The time has come. After 12 years of wearing the same pants four out of five days of the week and drinking lukewarm coffee from the break room, I’m retiring. I’ve truly loved working with you and appreciate every wild and wonderful day we shared.”.

According to recent reports, “Before I officially retire, I wanted to say thank you for this beautiful ride. You’ve all been unforgettable and lovely to me. You’re the reason this job didn’t feel like work.”.

“After 18 years, I’ve officially graduated to more peaceful days filled with puzzles and midday naps. Logging off now, grateful for every moment. I will miss you all!”.

Recent findings suggest that 💙 As you head into retirement, reflect on all the good times you had at work. Gratitude for the Day with Chibs Okereke can help you tap into those positive feelings.

It has been revealed that gratitude makes goodbye messages feel a little warmer. Think about the people or experiences that left a mark, like the coworker who knew your coffee order by heart or the one who always lent you their umbrella when it was raining. (If you need some more guidance, here are eight tips to cultivate an attitude of gratitude.).

“I want to thank my chosen family who made this workplace so special. Your support, humor, and occasional emergency snack stashes got me through some tough days and made the good ones even better.”.

“Thanks to everyone who made me feel welcome, challenged, and appreciated. You’re the reason I stayed as long as I did. Well, that, and Barbara’s famous cheesecake. I’ll miss you all (almost as much as I’ll miss all the cake).”.

“A heartfelt thank you to my team — you made me better every day. I’m so lucky I got to be a player on this incredible squad. Rooting for all of you always. Can’t wait to hear about all that you accomplish.”.

A little story can go a long way. In addition to reminding people of the good times, it can make your message feel more original. You don’t have to write a novel, and it doesn’t need to be profound — just aim for real.

“I’ll never forget the power outage of 2019 when we all played trashcan basketball while waiting for the lights to come back on. We made the best out of a tough situation, and that speaks to the type of amazing people you are. Please stay in touch!”.

“Monday mornings just won’t be the same without our doughnut runs. Thanks for the memories, team.”.

Sources indicate that let people know all that you’ve learned while working and what you’ll carry forward. Not only will this help fill up your cup, but it can also remind people what they’ve learned while working with you. (Here are 20 questions to help with any potential writer’s block.).

Recent findings suggest that “This job taught me a lot about leadership, teamwork, and that I don’t need to talk louder while I’m on zoom. (Still working on that one…) But most of all, it reminded me how amazing it is to work with such loyal, thoughtful people. I’ll never forget it. Thank you.”.

“Beyond the spreadsheets and deadlines, I’m leaving with lifelong friendships, a few more well-earned wrinkles, and countless memories.”.

“This place taught me how to lead, how to listen, and how to troubleshoot a broken coffee machine under pressure.”.

Some words of encouragement, a simple goodbye, or even a little glimpse of what’s next for you can be a sweet way to sign off.

“I’m off to spend more time traveling, playing with my grandkids, and mastering the art of sourdough once and for all. Wishing you all continued success — and a little less time in meetings.”.

“Wishing you all smooth releases, strong coffee, and at least one good laugh a day. Keep crushing it.”.

According to recent reports, “I’ll be around — probably in sweatpants, gardening gloves, or both. Don’t be a stranger.”.

💙 Consider listening to Endings with Tamara Levitt if you’re having a hard time saying goodbye to your work and the people you’ve met there.

It has been revealed that it can be tempting to sneak out, but saying farewell to your coworkers is a kind thing to do — and it can help you too. Here’s why:.

According to recent reports, 1. It gives you closure on your terms: Retirement can be a tough transition. One day, you have 50 emails and several meetings, and the next, your inbox is at zero, and you have nothing but time on your hands. Writing a goodbye message can help you mark the transition.

According to recent reports, 2. It opens the door for real connection: When you write a farewell message, you’re inviting people to respond. What better way to leave than by clearly seeing the impact you had on your coworkers?

In a recent development, 3. It lets you shape your own legacy: Your goodbye message can be a tiny chance to shape how people remember you. Go out on a positive note — literally.

It has been revealed that 💙 Writing to a coworker who’s retiring? These retirement wishes can help you find the right words.

Sources indicate that an announcement and a goodbye note do different jobs. The announcement shares your news and your last day. The thank-yous and memories from the tips above can follow it.

Manager first: Tell your manager before anyone else, so the news doesn’t reach them through a group email.

Timing: If you can, send the announcement a few weeks before your last day so people have time to say goodbye.

Subject line: Use a clear one, like “My retirement news.”.

Opening lines: Lead with the news, then name who will cover your work.

Long tenure: If you’ve been at the firm for decades, add a sentence or two about your time there, and keep the news first.

According to recent reports, here’s an example for someone who’s been at a manufacturer for a long time: “I started here 30 years ago, and my last day will be March 31. Over the next few weeks, I’ll be handing off my projects to Marcus and wrapping up my open work. If you’d like to catch up before I go, please grab time on my calendar. I’d love to see as many of you as I can.”.

Industry observers note that you don’t have to send a retirement message, but it can be one of the simplest ways to wrap up this chapter with a bit of closure and grace. After all, you’ve spent a lot of time with these people over the years.

Writing a short, thoughtful message can help you leave on a kind note. You might also be surprised at how meaningful even a few lines can feel, both for you and the people reading them.

There’s no one right way to send a retirement message. If you want to keep it casual, you could say something like, “After 15 years, I’m off to find out if daytime TV lives up to the hype. Thanks for the talks, laughs, and memories.”.

A more heartfelt message you could send is: “It’s been a true honor to work alongside so many talented people. I’m leaving with deep gratitude for my time here — and for all of you.”.

If humor’s more your vibe, you could say: “Today’s my last day. Thanks for the memories — and for being so nice about the fact that I was always muted on Zoom. You’d think after a few years, I’d learn my lesson, but I digress. You’re the best, and I’ll miss you.”.

Your tone depends on your personality and your workplace culture. If you’re in a very professional environment, a more formal message is the best way to go, but if your usual emails include memes and inside jokes, it’s okay to joke around.

In general, the best retirement messages usually sound like the person writing them, so trust your voice and just be yourself. You’ve earned the right to say goodbye on your terms.

There isn’t a standard checklist, but here are a few good touchpoints that can help you find your flow:.

Mention a funny or heartfelt memory.

Share a bit about what you’ve learned on the job.

Consider sprinkling in your future prepares.

Close with a simple and warm goodbye.

In a recent development, yes. Email is often preferred in the workplace, as it allows you to reach everyone and provides people with an opportunity to reply.

Whether you send it to your whole team or just a few close coworkers, an email is a low-stress, high-impact way to say farewell. Just remember to hit “send” before IT cuts your access!

If you’re retiring, your thank-you message to colleagues works best when it notes who you’re thanking and what they did for you. You can add it to your retirement announcement or send it as a separate note.

For the whole team, a few lines are enough: “Thank you all for the patience and the laughs. Working with this team has been the best part of my job.” For one person, name something specific: “Dana, thank you for answering my questions in my first year. I couldn’t have learned this job without you.” If coworkers gave you a send-off or a gift, a short note afterward can say thanks again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The unemployment rate for workers with autism is staggering. One Australian organization is aiming to change that.

In a recent development, in Australia, the unemployment rate for neurodivergent adults hovers around 34%, nearly eight times the national average. Clearly, there is a stigma around hiring neurodivergent people and it stems from a fear of the unknown. One not-for-profit manufacturer, Australian Spatial Analytics (ASA), is working to fix that.

In a recent development, ASA was established in 2020 to increase workforce participation among young neurodivergent adults by training them in significant data for the geospatial and digital engineering fields, then placing them in corporate and government sectors. At ASA, we leverage these employees’ cognitive strengths — attention to detail, pattern recognition, laser-sharp focus, and innovative problem-solving skills, all of which are invaluable in these fields.

About 80% of ASA’s staff identify as neurodivergent, which includes ADHD, autism, dyslexia, dyscalculia, and dyspraxia. ASA’s recruitment process goes beyond conventional practices; it assesses potential candidates based on transferable skills, hobbies, and interests, rather than relying on formal qualifications or previous experience. Many of the new data analysts we have successfully placed in jobs are in paid positions for the first time.

[Read: We’re Hiring – ADHD-Friendly Careers].

Yet the analysts’ value to their employers is without questions. Executives have praised the ASA-trained analysts who have joined their companies, citing their work ethic, dedication, and problem-solving skills.

It has been revealed that during the job-seeking process, ASA provides candidates with sample interview questions 48 hours in advance to help minimize anxiety. Once hired, employees receive comprehensive and paid on-the-job training that includes soft skills like communication and self-advocacy coaching.

[Read: Nail Your Job Interview – 3 Strategies for Neurodivergent Applicants].

Industry observers note that based on our experience, creating a supportive and productive environment requires only minor accommodations. Flexible start and finish times, predictable routines, the option for hybrid work to reduce commuting stress, adjustable lighting, noise-canceling headphones, and direct communication make a profound difference, not only for neurodivergent people, but for everyone in the workplace.

Recent findings suggest that to help change paradigms, ASA offers a Neurodiversity in the Workplace Training Program for other organizations. It covers neurodiversity awareness, plus effective strategies for communication, managing anxiety in the work environment, leading neurodiverse teams, and promoting neurodivergent inclusion.

Ultimately, our goal is to put ourselves out of business.

Karly Ischenko is a Human Resources Business Partner at Australian Spatial Analytics.

Smith & Diction rebuilt the PHS brand identity around a Bloom logo, with three plants growing from the letters and Philadelphia grid underneath.

The old mark was a tree in a circle, and it mentioned too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees. The Pennsylvania Horticultural Society tends gardens and parks across the Philadelphia region and runs the Flower Show. The fresh mark keeps the letters PHS as the foundation and grows three plants out of them, each drawn by Summer McClure to fit a Philadelphia city block. In deep green and burgundy on cream, mint, and sky blue, with dozens of colors in the palette, the identity looks like a garden because it behaves like one: every visit shows something new.

Recent findings suggest that the wordmark is custom, built to hold the plants like roots hold a stem. The supporting type comes from the societyâs own archive: old exhibition posters that were beautiful and hardworking, no frills, just type. Caslon Doric leads, with the confidence and clean legibility of classic newspaper headlines, and ES Park backs it up, a slab serif with geometric moments and measured softness.

Underneath it all sits William Pennâs original city grid. The studio baked the grid into the logo itself, then extended it through every print layout, matching the grid to the width of the flowers. Like beds in a garden, the structure keeps everything in place while each layout keeps its own personality. The mark never sits still: Henrique Barone hand-drew every frame of the plants growing, and Justin Lawes made a version that sways with the breeze.

Recent findings suggest that this is a brand made to be held, not just seen. The studio printed a 42-page brand book, made a matte gold lapel pin of the mark, and built a flip book that shows the logo growing frame by frame. They matched paper tones to nearly every brand color, so the team can print in-house and stay on brand. The book cover carries the Bloom logo in dark green on mint, with an orange seal.

The floral illustrations do more than decorate. Each one stands for a part of the organization: a flower in a cocktail glass for the Pop Up Gardens, a leafy radish for the community gardens, an oak leaf for the Healthy Neighborhoods program, a branching tree for the McLean Library. The library also gives the 2027 Philadelphia Flower Show its own peony mark, while Bre Furlongâs photographs of 18 flowers, including the tulip the studio calls the Ballerina, carry the ICONIC theme in Herbus type.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 50% of people receiving treatment for eating disorders, especially bulimia and binge-eating, may have ADHD, though few are diagnosed, according to a upcoming study.

Roughly half of adults in treatment for eating disorders display symptoms of ADHD, though few are diagnosed, according to a new cross-sectional study published in Journal of Eating Disorders.1.

Recent findings suggest that the study, conducted at Esquirol Hospital in Limoges, France, included 120 participants, 95.8% of whom were female. Using the ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS v1.1), researchers screened participants for ADHD, then followed up to confirm the screening with the Diagnostic Interview for ADHD (DIVA 2.0). More than half (61) of the participants met criteria for ADHD, according to these measures, though only two had received a prior diagnosis. Bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder were more strongly associated with ADHD than was anorexia nervosa.

Participants who highlighted symptoms of ADHD also had more psychiatric comorbidities and higher rates of impulsivity, body dissatisfaction, and smoking and alcohol use. Personality assessments revealed that participants with ADHD symptoms showed greater dependence on rewards, while those who did not exhibited higher rates of self-regulation.

“These findings support ADHD screening and integrated treatments targeting impulsivity and attentional dysregulation,” wrote the study’s authors.

In “ADHD and Eating Disorders: Research, Diagnosis & Treatment Guidelines,” Roberto Olivardia, Ph.D., explores the myriad biological and genetic factors that may predispose individuals with ADHD to eating disorders. They include:.

Further research is needed to understand all possible mechanisms, as well as the benefit of ADHD treatment on eating disorder recovery.

Industry observers note that in an ADDitude guest blog post titled, “Dopamine, Not Discipline: The ADHD–Eating Disorder Link I Was Missing,” Penelope Mazzetti offers these insights: “My ‘out-of-control eating’ wasn’t an problem of willpower; it was partly sensory-seeking behavior, a well-documented ADHD trait. As ADHD brains like mine are chronically low in dopamine, we are wired to seek stimulation, and food just happens to be fast, legal, and always available.”.

Tech Report: Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (453 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, said:.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

Industry observers note that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. #137881. Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (782 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food.
  • But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?
  • Sources indicate that in a newly introduced study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity’s prosocial evolutionary past.

But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?

Sources indicate that in a newly introduced study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves. Closely bonded chimps swiped pineapple pieces from one another less frequently than those with weaker relationships. Additionally, victims were quicker to calm down when the thief was a friend, and thieves indicated less hostility when stealing from a bonded pal than from a non-friend.

The upcoming research deepens our understanding of the emotional underpinnings of our social lives, stated Oded Ritov, the paper’s first author and a Berkeley psychology Ph.D. student.

Sources indicate that “Collaborative relationships are crucial for our well-being, health, and survival,” said Ritov, who works with Berkeley’s Social Origins Lab. “Increasingly, we’re understanding that this isn’t something that’s unique to us, but that other animals have friends, as well.”.

The paper was published online in September and will appear in the November concern of the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

Scientists are sometimes hesitant to describe an apparently close relationship between chimps as akin to human friendship, arguing that we can’t grasp their cognitive and emotional complexity. To identify those who showed signs of a close relationship, researchers observed 26 chimps for more than 800 hours at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. The team documented which chimps appeared to be closely bonded—like friends—by taking note of their grooming patterns, daily interactions, and how regularly they were within arm’s reach of others.

In a recent development, then they set up two rooms. One contained a “victim” chimp with three trays baited with pineapple. Researchers attached a rope to the trays and led it into the other room, where a second chimp—the thief—could either leave the rope alone or yank it to steal the pineapple.

In a recent development, chimps stole in 70% of trials with non-friends, compared with 61% of trials with friends. While 9 percentage points may not seem large, each chimp experienced both friend and non-friend conditions, a methodological technique that leads to a higher degree of confidence that the difference is meaningful and not just random chance.

“Ours is the first study to show that they’re able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” Ritov noted.

Industry observers note that researchers also measured how the victims responded to being stolen from by evaluating their stomping, fist-pounding, and screeching. Victims were initially angrier when friends stole from them but quickly moderated their feelings compared with when non-friends stole from them.

In a recent development, the thieves’ behavior also changed. When non-friends were the thieves, the thieves expressed negative emotions for much longer, suggesting they viewed the interaction as more hostile.

“This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans,” Ritov noted.

Jan Engelmann, an associate professor of psychology and principal investigator with the Social Origins Lab, said previous work has shown relationship-specific intentions in nonhuman primates. But human friendships are about more than special intentions, he added—they’re about stronger expectations.

According to recent reports, “We expect more of our friends,” remarked Engelmann, a senior author of the paper. “These findings really deepen our understanding of the evolutionary roots of friendships. This is, to my knowledge, the first evidence showing that also chimpanzees expect and maybe demand special treatment from their friends. These kinds of social expectations might form the basis of human moral principles.”.

In a recent development, the paper adds to Ritov’s work that focuses on the evolution of human behavior and how morals and norms are part of our core being, traceable to other animals. He has recently studied whether nonhuman animals have a sense of fairness and is broadly interested in how emotions unfold across cultures and species.

Industry observers note that “We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” Ritov remarked. “The expectations that chimpanzees have from their friends or close collaborative partners might have scaled up to more generalized expectations for how we should treat each other.”.

Jason Pohl is a science writer in UC Berkeley's Office of Communications & Public Affairs.
